a3_plaza: The counted city opens at the deep stair's foot: nine streets radiating from a plaza, nine hundred lamps, a great chapel on one side and a working mint on the other. Eleven thousand people live inside the arithmetic here. There is a fountain. There are children. There is a queue outside a municipal office, and the queue is orderly.
e_a3_plaza_1: The plaza is seen, the city counted at a glance, and the stair taken straight back up before anybody has crossed the square. It is the last moment at which this could still be called a reconnaissance. Everybody in the company knows that at the time, and four of them say so on the stair.
a3_chapel: The great chapel of Kar Ashen is Reckoning-built over dwarf foundations and holds four thousand. There is a service in progress. The entire congregation is counting in unison, in nines, in a rhythm the company has heard in a barn on the shelf road and in a barracks at Sixteen Mile and in a gallery under a moor.
a3_chapel_a: A full hour of a liturgy that is arithmetic set to plainsong, four thousand voices keeping a count in nines. At the end there is a form of words that names the debt, the term and the collateral, in that order. Nyre knows the tune. It is her own order's evening office with the numbers changed.
a3_chapel_b: A service interrupted from the aisle by a Warden charter, and a celebrant who stops mid-phrase, answers the question fully, and invites the captain to read the liturgy's colophon for himself. Then he resumes the count from exactly where he left it, and four thousand people come back in on the correct number.
e_a3_chapel_1: The celebrant is pressed in his own vestry about who wrote the liturgy, and he answers. The name is on a signed requisition in the company's own pack. Four thousand people are still counting on the other side of the vestry door, and the count does not falter when the door opens.
a3_choir: The choir loft above the nave holds nine cantors who keep the count for the whole city in shifts, and have kept it from that loft, without a break, since the founding. There are nine chairs. There is a water jug. There is a slate for the shift change, and the shift change is timed to the second.
a3_choir_a: The shift roll, read in a choir loft: nine hundred years of names in nine-hour shifts, four hundred pages of them. The last page lists next month's shifts, filled in as far as the twentieth, with nine blanks at the bottom. The blanks are ruled and waiting, and the ruling was done in the same ink.
e_a3_choir_1: The count is stopped in the great chapel of Kar Ashen for nine seconds by a hand over a cantor's mouth. The whole city hears it stop, because the whole city is keeping time to it. Eleven thousand people turn toward the chapel at once, and what they do next is not violent and is not slow.
a3_confessor: The chapel's confessor is an old man with a lifetime of the city's private arithmetic in his head. He will talk to a Warden company because he has been waiting forty years for somebody official to ask, and he says so before anybody has asked. He has a chair set out for it, and a jug, and a pen.
a3_confessor_a: Four hours in a confessional with a man who has kept a city's secrets professionally, and who gives up all of them at once in a flat voice, in order, with dates. Ilsabet writes as fast as she can and misses none of it. At the end he asks whether that was useful, and then asks it again.
a3_confessor_b: The crown clerk is named: it is an office, not a person, held for nine hundred years by a succession of holders. The current one is a man the confessor christened himself, forty-one years ago, and has confessed every ninth day since. He gives the name, the house, and the hours at which he can be found.
e_a3_confessor_1: The confessor is asked to name the fallen-behind families out loud in his own chapel, and he does it, all four hundred of them, in order, from memory, over the course of an hour. The ninth name in the list is his own, and he says it in the same voice as the other three hundred and ninety-nine.
a3_relic: The chapel reliquary of the counted city holds eight tally-irons on velvet in a case built for nine. Under the ninth setting there is a plate, engraved, and the engraving is not yet complete: an office, a date this spring, and a space for a name. The burr is still on the letters.
a3_relic_a: The ninth plate, read through glass: an office, a term of nine years, a date this spring, and a blank where a name goes. The engraver stopped at the blank rather than leaving the whole plate for later, which means the office was expected to be filled and the filling was expected to be soon.
a3_relic_b: One founding iron comes off the velvet in a chapel with four thousand people in it, and nobody stops it. Two of the cantors watch the whole thing from the loft without breaking the count. Afterwards there are two empty settings in the case, and the plate under the ninth is still not finished.
e_a3_relic_1: A reliquary case is broken in the great chapel and all eight founding irons are taken at once, which is the entire holding tally of a door somewhere in this mountain. The city's response is not violence. It is a bell, rung once, and then the whole congregation standing up together and turning round.
a3_mint: The mint of Kar Ashen is working: nine hearths, a rolling floor, gauge benches, eighty smiths on shift. At the far end the crown die stands under a hood on a dwarf anvil, with two of the crown clerk's household beside it who are not smiths and are not armed and do not appear to do anything at all.
a3_mint_a: The coal yard at shift change is forty smiths going out and forty coming in, and five strangers crossing a mint floor in the middle of it with nobody looking at anything except their own hands. It works because a mint at shift change is the least observant place in any city, including this one.
a3_mint_b: The mint is entered openly on a Warden charter, which the mint-master reads, accepts and files. Then he shows the company the floor himself, at length, with professional pride, because there is nothing on it he considers illegal and he has never been told that anybody thinks otherwise.
a3_mint_c: Kettle goes over the mint roof and down into the die room's clerestory, which takes forty minutes and a great deal of patience. It puts one member of the company inside the only room in Kar Ashen that actually matters, with a view of the die, the rack, and the two who stand beside them.
e_a3_mint_1: The crown die is demanded on Warden authority in a working mint in front of eighty smiths. The two of the household beside it step back rather than forward, which is the first warning. The eighty smiths put down their tools and form up in nines, which is the second, and there is no third.
a3_dies: The die room holds the crown die bolted to a dwarf anvil under a hood, four cut irons cooling in a rack beside it, and a ledger on a stand listing what has been cut this season and what is still to cut. The hood is up. The ledger is open. Everything in the room is exactly where the rota says it should be.
a3_dies_a: A cut iron off the cooling rack, founding gauge, still warm through a glove. Its tally matches the crown door's own ring, which Ilsabet establishes in four minutes with a wire and a rubbing. Its flank is blank where a name goes, and the blank has been filed smooth in readiness.
a3_dies_b: The season's cutting ledger, read at the stand: nine irons cut, eight distributed to the ring, and the ninth entered as held pending the appointment of a hand. The entry is dated eleven days ago. It is the day the slag heap went cold, and the day the pump house's maintenance hand changed.
e_a3_dies_1: The crown die is unbolted from its anvil in the middle of a working mint: forty pounds of dwarf steel that decides what every iron in this mountain says. The mint stops. All eighty of them stop at once, without a signal, and turn round, and the room is a hundred feet long with one door.
a3_smiths: The mint's smiths are eighty people who have cut irons here father to daughter for nine hundred years, and their foreman would like to know what a Warden company thinks it is doing on his floor. He asks it reasonably. He is holding a two-pound hammer while he asks, because he was using it.
a3_smiths_a: Eleven minutes of fighting across a mint floor against people who work with hammers for a living, in a room with nine open hearths in it. It reaches the far door. It costs blood, and it costs the company any possibility of ever being welcome in this city again, and it does not get anybody the die.
a3_smiths_b: An argument with a mint foreman conducted entirely in trade terms: gauge, tally, warrant and standing order. He wins two points of it. He loses the third, which is whether a standing order signed by an office rather than a person can be produced on request, and he stands aside and writes down that he did.
a3_smiths_c: A blank is cut for the company on the crown die by a foreman who has been asked correctly, in trade form, with the gauge specified. He does it because the request was made properly and the die does not care whose hand pulls the lever. He also, unasked, files the flank smooth.
e_a3_smiths_1: A hearth's oil store is fired to make smoke to escape in, in a mint with nine working hearths and nine hundred years of oil in its floor seams. The smoke works. What the smoke does not do is confuse eighty people who know exactly which of the two doors anybody would run for.
e_a3_smiths_2: A return is made across a cleared mint floor for the die, on the reasonable grounds that the fight has already been had. The second shift is coming in through the coal yard door at the ninth hour with the whole household behind it, and the company is standing at an anvil with a spanner in its hands.
a3_blanks: The blank store behind the mint holds nine hundred years of uncut blanks in dwarf bins, sorted by gauge, and a ledger of issues going back to the founding. There are four entries for this spring. They are in a hand the company has seen on requisitions at Rell's Gate and on a chart at Sarnhold.
a3_blanks_a: Four spring issues, read at the store's own desk: three to the ring, and one to a name that Nyre stops reading aloud halfway through. It is the legate who came up to Sarnhold with a coach and a writ to take custody of the company's irons for safekeeping, and the issue predates his arrival by a month.
e_a3_blanks_1: The issue ledger is burned in a dwarf blank store to destroy the record, which takes four minutes and works completely. It also destroys the only document connecting a mother-house legate to a mint under a mountain. The company understands that about four minutes after the last page has gone.
a3_market: The market of the counted is a market like any market, with bread and iron and cloth, except for the ninth stall in every row. The ninth stall sells nothing. It has a clerk at it and a ledger and a queue, and the queue moves briskly, and people thank the clerk when they reach the front of it.
a3_market_a: An hour in the queue at a stall that sells nothing. Eleven people in turn give the clerk a name, receive a token, and thank him. The twelfth is a child on her own, who gives a name that is not hers, receives the token, and carries it away in both hands as though it were hot.
a3_market_b: Food, rope and lamp oil bought at fair prices in a market under a mountain, from people who make change correctly and wish the company a good afternoon. Eleven thousand people go about their day around it. The whole transaction takes twenty minutes and is the most disturbing twenty minutes in the book.
e_a3_market_1: The ninth stall is cleared and its queue sent home by a Warden company acting on a charter. The queue goes home. It comes back at the ninth hour. The stall is staffed again by then with a different clerk and the same ledger, and the day's entries have all been made up from the tokens already issued.
a3_pens: The pens below the market are for stock, and they hold stock. The ninth pen holds nine people, fed and warm, with their households' tokens on cords around their necks. There is straw. There is a water trough with a cover on it. The stockman keeps all nine pens to the same standard and is proud of it.
a3_pens_a: The ninth pen is opened, and nine people stay in it. The eldest explains to a Warden captain, with real patience and no bitterness at all, why leaving would cost nine other households their tokens, and what happens to a household without a token, and how long it takes.
a3_pens_b: Eleven minutes over a rail with nine people who are calm, informed and entirely uninterested in being rescued. What they want is for the company to carry a letter down to a family at the eighth station. They have written it already. It is four lines long and it is not about them.
a3_pens_c: The ninth pen is bought outright from the stockman at market rate, receipted, with nine tokens handed over and nine names struck from a book. It takes eleven minutes and empties the company's purse entirely. The stockman gives a proper receipt and asks whether the company wants the pen as well.
e_a3_pens_1: The stockman is cut down in his own pens for a set of keys. He is one man with a stick, and it takes four seconds. He was also a father of four, the pens are municipal property, and the hue and cry closes nine streets between the market and the deep stair within the quarter hour.
e_a3_pens_2: The youngest of the ninth pen is carried out over her own objection and her household's. Her household's tokens are struck the same afternoon, because a pen short at the count is arrears. The eight who remain make up the difference, and they were told that would happen, and they told the company so.
a3_auction: The arrears auction is held on the ninth of every month in a hall off the market, and it is held with perfect courtesy. Households that have fallen behind bid their own names against each other for another month's grace. There is a rostrum, a clerk, and a bell. Nine hundred people attend, and most of them are not bidding.
a3_auction_a: An hour at the back of an arrears auction, conducted throughout with the manners of a livestock sale in a good market town. Four names are sold. Two of them are bought by the crown clerk's own household, which bids by paddle, and which does not bid against itself, and which pays over the odds both times.
a3_auction_b: Every lot is bid on until the purse is empty, which buys four households a month of grace and costs the company everything it has. It also raises the reserve on every remaining lot, because the room has now learned that there is outside money in it, and the auctioneer adjusts accordingly and apologises for doing so.
e_a3_auction_1: An arrears auction is broken up from the floor by a Warden company, and it adjourns politely, with the auctioneer thanking the company for its attendance. It reconvenes at the ninth hour in the chapel undercroft with the same lots, plus nine more, and the nine more are the households that spoke up in the hall.
a3_ledgers: The auction hall's ledgers fill nine hundred years of shelving, one volume per decade, recording every name sold in this city since the founding. It is a continuous record in a single institutional hand. There is an index. There is a reading desk. There is a lamp with a shade on it for readers.
a3_ledgers_a: A century of arrears read in ninety minutes by two people taking notes: the rate, the cycle, the household names, and the one fact that matters most. The rate has doubled since Kar Duhn shut, and doubled again since Hollowmarch, which means the company's own two books are in this ledger as a cause.
e_a3_ledgers_1: The auction ledger's hand is held against a Reckoning requisition from the company's own pack, in front of the hall clerk, on his own desk. The two hands match. The hall clerk looks at both of them for a long moment, and then quietly leaves the room, and does not come back with what he went for.
a3_archive: The city archive occupies nine floors of dwarf shelving with nine hundred years of Kar Ashen's arithmetic on it, four archivists, and a public reading room. It is entirely open to any citizen who asks. There is a request slip. There is a trolley. There is a rule about not taking lamps between the stacks.
a3_archive_a: A request for everything on the crown door is filled in forty minutes by an archivist who brings eleven boxes on a trolley and asks, on the way past, whether the company would like the founding volume as well, since most people who ask for the boxes turn out to want the volume.
e_a3_archive_1: Nine floors of dwarf shelving are set alight to end an arithmetic. The arithmetic survives, because it is kept in nine places and this is one of them. What does not survive is a city's own history of itself, and the company is remembered for exactly that, correctly, for as long as anybody remembers anything.
a3_stacks: The founding volume is kept in a dwarf vault at the bottom of nine floors, behind a door that has stood open for nine hundred years. The step into it has been worn into a groove. There is a lectern, a chair, and a lamp bracket, and the bracket has a lamp in it that is lit.
a3_stacks_a: Four hours in a dwarf vault with the founding volume, and it is not a contract. It is a set of engineering specifications. It describes the doors as containment, the count as a maintenance schedule, and the hands as an operating crew, and it does all of that in the flat prose of people writing for successors.
a3_stacks_b: Nine clauses copied in Ilsabet's shorthand, which is the smallest defensible extract and the one an inquiry will actually read. It takes an hour rather than four. She copies the clause numbers, the volume's shelf mark and the vault's own catalogue number as well, because she has been thinking about courts since Hollowmarch.
e_a3_stacks_1: The founding volume is taken out of its vault, which the archive permits, because the archive permits any citizen to borrow. The archive's standing order also requires the borrowing to be reported to the crown clerk within the hour, along with the borrower's name, and the archivist fills the slip in while the company watches.
a3_index: The archive's index is kept on nine thousand slips in nine cabinets, cross-referenced by name, household and year. Any citizen can use it. The system is simple, well maintained, and entirely comprehensive, and it works in both directions, which is a property of indexes that nobody in the company has thought about before today.
a3_index_a: Five names looked up in a nine-thousand-slip index, and all five found, with arrival dates. Behind them, filed in the same drawer in the same hand, there is a sixth slip. It has the company's number on it, a date this week, and a cross-reference to a shelf mark in the crown ledger's own series.
e_a3_index_1: The index is consulted for the crown clerk's office holders, which produces nine slips in good order. In the same drawer there is a tenth slip, blank except for a date and two words. The words are pending appointment. The date is today, and the slip has been in that drawer since before the company reached the gate.
a3_archivist: The senior archivist has been in this building fifty years, knows exactly what her archive is, and has spent her whole professional life keeping it complete against the possibility of a day like this one. She says that in the first minute. She has a folder ready, with tabs in it, and the folder is not thin.
a3_archivist_a: Nine certified copies made, sealed and signed by an archivist of fifty years' standing, with her office stamp and her personal seal on each one. In a Warden court it is worth more than everything else the company has picked up in three books put together, and she makes ten and keeps one herself.
a3_archivist_b: The answer of somebody who has read all of it: the count is a maintenance schedule for a containment, the containment has been maintained, and she would like the company to understand that she is not defending it. She says the last part twice, and then asks whether that was clear, and asks it again later.
e_a3_archivist_1: An archivist of fifty years' standing is asked to come down a mountain and testify, and she agrees, and goes to pack a bag. She is entered in the ninth column before the company reaches the wyrm gate, which takes about four hours, and her folder is back on its shelf by the following morning.
a3_aqueduct: The city aqueduct brings warm water down from somewhere above the crown door and runs the whole lower city on it. There is an inspection walkway along its channel, with markers every hundred yards. The water is warm enough to steam in the lamplight, and it is the reason the baths exist, and the mills, and the eels.
a3_aqueduct_a: A mile of inspection walkway upstream, the water getting warmer under the hand every hundred yards. At the ninth marker the channel's stonework changes: dwarf work below it, and above it something older and better, cut without tool marks, which Vurma looks at for a long time and declines to identify.
a3_aqueduct_b: The channel is crossed on a maintenance plank and the lower city entered from above, which is quieter and dirtier and puts the company among the uncounted rather than the counted. Nobody up here has a token. Nobody up here is in a column. It is the only part of Kar Ashen where anybody looks at strangers.
e_a3_aqueduct_1: A warm quiet channel is swum for a quarter mile because it is warm and quiet. The grating at the far end turns out to be a filter rather than a gate. What it filters is why the water below it is warm, and the swimming has been downstream of that filter for the whole quarter mile.
a3_sluice: The great sluice divides the aqueduct nine ways for the nine quarters, with a keeper's hut, nine gates and a log book. The keeper has held the gates for thirty years and knows every allocation by heart. He is pleased to have visitors and offers tea, and the tea is made with the aqueduct's own water.
a3_sluice_a: The keeper answers while he works, because the gates need working: upstream is the crown cistern, above the cistern is the door, and the water is warm because it comes off the door. It has always come off the door. His father told him that, and his father had it from the keeper before him.
a3_sluice_b: The ninth gate is shut, which dries one quarter in forty minutes. It brings not constables but nine householders with buckets, who ask the company, reasonably and with some embarrassment, to open it again, and who explain what the quarter uses that water for and how long the cisterns hold.
a3_sluice_c: Nine days of sluice log, read at the keeper's table: the same allocations every day, in the same hand. On the ninth day of each cycle the whole flow is diverted to the crown cistern for two hours. Tomorrow is a ninth day, and the diversion has already been entered, in advance, with the hours.
e_a3_sluice_1: Nine sluice gates are opened at once to flood nine quarters, which is nine hundred years of arithmetic drowned in an afternoon. It works exactly as intended. Eleven thousand people lose their homes to a company that came up here to help them, and the count is unaffected, because the count was never in the buildings.
e_a3_sluice_2: A sluice-keeper is asked what the water tastes of in the ninth week, and he answers honestly out of thirty years of tasting it, because a keeper tastes his water and that is the job. The company stands in his hut with his tea going cold in their hands and understands the aqueduct at last.
a3_mills: The mill row on the aqueduct runs nine mills, and eight of them are grinding grain. The ninth mill's stones are turning on nothing at all. Its miller stands outside in the lane because he will not go in while it is running, and he has not gone in while it is running for nine years.
a3_mills_a: The ninth mill entered with a miller who has not been inside it while it was working since he inherited it. It is grinding. It has a hopper. The hopper has been fed on the ninth of every month for as long as the mill has stood there, and the feeding is done by somebody else, at night.
a3_mills_b: The miller answers at his own door, plainly: the ninth mill grinds what the ninth column allots, the flour goes to the chapel, and he has never eaten the chapel's bread. Neither has his family. Neither, he says, has anybody on this row, and he would rather the company did not either.
a3_mills_c: The mill row is walked past at speed with nine wheels turning and one of them turning on nothing. It is the correct decision and it takes four minutes. Nobody in the company is able to leave it behind afterwards, and two of them raise it again that evening without meaning to.
e_a3_mills_1: The ninth mill's wheel is stopped by a company that has had enough. That stops the chapel's bread, which stops the liturgy's own offering, which stops the count at the evening office. The crown clerk's household is on the mill row within the hour, and it does not arrive angry, which is worse.
e_a3_mills_2: A look into the ninth mill's hopper, taken deliberately by somebody who had been told what was in it and needed to see for himself. The hopper is full. The mill goes on working while the looking happens, because a mill does, and nobody standing on that floor is able to move for eleven seconds.
a3_quiet: A dwarf rest-house stands on the mill row: empty, clean, nine beds, a stove laid ready, kept by the city for travellers because the city keeps everything properly. There is a book to sign. There is a jug of the aqueduct's water on the table, and nobody in the company touches it.
a3_quiet_a: Four hours in a warm dwarf rest-house on clean beds, taken deliberately by a company that has learned three books' worth of lessons about arriving at doors tired. Nobody signs the book. Everybody sleeps, and Kettle takes both watches and does not tell anybody until afterwards.
a3_wardens: The city's Warden post exists. It is manned by six Wardens of a garrison posted here nine years ago, who have heard nothing from Sarnhold since, and who come to attention when they see a charter because they have been waiting nine years to have a reason to. Their uniforms are mended and clean.
a3_wardens_a: Six Wardens brought under a Commandant's written orders, who fall in gratefully and badly. They have not drilled in nine years. They will be a liability everywhere on this mountain except in front of the crown door, and their sergeant knows both halves of that and volunteers anyway.
a3_wardens_b: The answer comes from a sergeant who has drafted eleven reports in nine years and sent every one of them. They went down with the couriers, on the schedule, because the couriers are the post. The schedule is the crown clerk's. None of the eleven ever arrived, and he has kept the drafts.
e_a3_wardens_1: A whole Warden post is arrested for dereliction by a chartered company, which is legally sound and practically insane. It puts six men in their own cells. It also puts the company on the crown clerk's list twice over, once as arresting officers and once as the only Wardens now unaccounted for in the city.
a3_gibbets: The gibbet row in the ninth street is where the counted city hangs its criminals, and nine cages hang there. Eight are occupied. The ninth stands open with a step under it and a plate on it that has not been filled in. The cages are clean, and the row is swept, and there is a rail for the public.
a3_gibbets_a: Eight plates read in order: eight names, eight crimes, and every one of the crimes the same crime, which is refusing an entry in the ninth column. All eight are dated within the last two months. The oldest of them is dated eleven days after Hollowmarch, which is when the rate doubled.
e_a3_gibbets_1: Eight gibbet cages are cut down in the ninth street of a city of eleven thousand, which is a public act performed in public. The city does not treat it as a rescue. It treats it as arrears, because eight cages empty at the count is eight entries short, and arrears fall on whoever is standing nearest.
a3_kennels: The city kennels hold the crown clerk's household's hounds. They are not hounds. The kennel-master is the only man in Kar Ashen who goes armed as a matter of routine, and he is armed with a stick, a horn and a set of keys, which tells the company what he is actually for.
a3_kennels_a: The kennel-master is killed at his own door, which takes eleven seconds because he is one man with a stick. It leaves the company standing between an open kennel and a street with nine hundred people in it, holding a set of keys nobody in the company knows the order of.
a3_kennels_b: The kennels are passed along the wall at the pace of a funeral. Nine of them come to the bars in order as the company goes by, one after another, keeping pace on the inside. None of them makes any sound at all, and that is the part Kettle mentions afterwards, twice.
a3_kennels_c: The charter is shown to a kennel-master who reads it and answers without embarrassment: they are for households that run. There have been nine this year. None of the nine got further than the second street, and he does not say that as a boast, and he does not appear to think it is one.
e_a3_kennels_1: The crown clerk's kennels are opened by a company acting on principle, in a city with nine hundred people in the street outside. Nine of them go into that street ahead of anybody's ability to warn it. What follows is not the company's fault in intention and is entirely the company's fault in fact.
e_a3_kennels_2: A decision is taken to go into the kennels and finish what is in them, which is nine of them in a stone run eleven feet wide with one door. It is the last tactical decision anybody in the Ninth Sword makes on this street, and it is made by people who know better and do it anyway.
a3_cages: The cage yard behind the kennels holds nine transport cages on wheels. Four are loaded and sealed for the ninth-hour delivery. A manifest is chained to the yard gate, weather-proofed under a slate, and the yard has been swept, and the cages' wheels have been greased this week.
a3_cages_a: The manifest, read at the gate: four cages, nine names, a delivery time and a destination. The destination is the crown door itself, at the ninth hour tomorrow. The names are entered in the household form, with ages, and two of them are ages the company would rather not have read.
a3_cages_b: Four sealed transport cages are broken open in a yard behind the kennels, and nine people get out. All nine ask, immediately and unanimously, to be put back in before the yard's own count is taken. They are not hysterical about it. They explain the arithmetic, twice, and then they ask again.
e_a3_cages_1: The company rides up to the crown door inside a sealed transport cage on the ninth-hour delivery, in place of the nine, which is an excellent plan for arriving. It has no provision whatsoever for the arrival, or for the fact that a sealed cage is sealed from the outside by people who count.
a3_baths: The city baths are dwarf-built, fed off the warm aqueduct, open to any citizen and full at midday. They are also indifferent to a Warden company standing filthy in the doorway with four days of the spine on it. There is a rail for kit. There is soap. There is an attendant who asks nothing.
a3_baths_a: An hour in a dwarf bath fed by water that comes off the crown door, which nobody enjoys once Vurma says that sentence out loud, and which gets four days of the spine off five people regardless. Everybody is cleaner. Nobody is comfortable. Ilsabet washes twice and does not explain why.
a3_surgeon: The city surgeon is competent, has set the company's kind of injuries before, and wants nothing in return except that somebody official finally write down what she has spent nineteen years treating. She says so while she is laying out instruments, without looking up, in the tone of somebody who has rehearsed it.
a3_surgeon_a: Two hours with a competent surgeon: Dellach's forearm resewn properly, Mira's ankle strapped, everybody's frostbite dressed and two of Kettle's fingers splinted. The company is genuinely capable again for the first time since the pass, which is worth more than anything else in this city.
a3_surgeon_b: A surgeon's statement, taken and witnessed: nineteen years of injuries, their pattern, their timing, and the nine cases a year that arrive on the tenth of the month having spent a night in a cage. She signs it. She asks for a copy. She puts the copy in her own case file where it will be found.
e_a3_surgeon_1: A city surgeon is refused on the assumption that she reports to the ward, which she does, honestly and openly, because that is her post. Her ward return for the day therefore records a Warden company that declined treatment and looked ill, with a description, and the return goes up at the hour.
a3_beds: The surgeon's ward holds nine beds. Eight have patients in them. The ninth is made up with a chart already hanging on its rail and a name written on the chart in a clerk's hand, and the bed has been made up like that, with that chart, since before the company came down the deep stair.
a3_beds_a: The ninth chart, read off its rail: a name, an age, an admission date of tomorrow, and a treatment plan consisting of the single word none. The hand is the one that has signed every requisition in the company's pack. The name is one of the nine on the cage yard's manifest.
e_a3_beds_1: A chart is taken off a ward rail, which the surgeon reports, because a missing chart is a missing patient and she is required to account for both. The company's own description goes into a city report at the exact hour it most needed not to be in one, and the report is copied twice.
a3_wyrmgate: The wyrm gate stands at the counted city's lowest street, a dwarf arch with the whole city's warm air going up through it and nine lamps burning on it. There is no guard. There has never been a guard. Beyond it the wyrm-road goes down along Ashendrel's own flank, and it is nine miles long.
